units.title: RELATIONSHIPS

overview.intro: This unit is about the people around you — how friendships start, how they break, and how they get repaired. At C1 level the challenge is no longer describing people, but talking about relationships with nuance: hedging, softening, and disagreeing without causing offence.
goals: Describe how relationships begin, change and end using phrasal verbs naturally.
Choose correctly between gerund and infinitive after common verbs.
Disagree politely and hold your position in a discussion.
overview.outcome: By the end you can tell a detailed anecdote about a friendship over time, and take part in a disagreement using at least three softening expressions.

vocab.def: a person you know slightly, but who is not a close friend.
vocab.use: Use it when ‘friend’ would be too strong — a workmate you chat with, a neighbour you greet in the lift.
examples: She’s an acquaintance from my old job, not someone I’d call at midnight.
We were acquaintances for two years before we became real friends.
vocab.colloc: a mutual acquaintance · a business acquaintance · a passing acquaintance

vocab.def: to like someone and become friendly the moment you meet.
vocab.use: Almost always used with ‘straight away / immediately’, and the object is always ‘it’ — never ‘hit off him’.
examples: We hit it off straight away and talked for three hours.
They didn’t hit it off at first, but now they’re inseparable.
vocab.colloc: hit it off immediately · hit it off with someone · really hit it off

vocab.def: to argue and stop being friendly with someone.
vocab.use: The reason takes ‘over’: you fall out WITH a person OVER a thing. The opposite is ‘make up’.
examples: I fell out with my cousin over an inheritance.
They fell out years ago and never made up.
vocab.colloc: fall out with someone · fall out over money · a falling-out (noun)

vocab.def: to agree completely with someone.
vocab.use: Most common in the negative: ‘we don’t see eye to eye on…’ is a diplomatic way of admitting disagreement.
examples: We don’t see eye to eye on politics, so we avoid the subject.
On money matters we’ve always seen eye to eye.
vocab.colloc: see eye to eye with someone · see eye to eye on something

vocab.def: to give a certain impression to other people.
vocab.use: About the impression given, not the reality — so it pairs well with ‘although in fact…’.
examples: He comes across as arrogant, although he’s actually shy.
In interviews, try to come across as confident but humble.
vocab.colloc: come across as rude / friendly / confident · come across well

vocab.def: a polite, slightly formal way of saying you disagree.
vocab.use: Use it in a meeting or debate when you want to push back firmly but stay courteous. It sounds odd in casual chat with close friends.
examples: I’m afraid I beg to differ — the data suggests the opposite.
You say the plan is safe; I beg to differ.
vocab.colloc: I beg to differ · I’d beg to differ on that point

vocab.def: to begin a conversation or friendship, often by chance.
vocab.use: Separable but rarely split: “strike up a conversation with a stranger”.
examples: We struck up a friendship on the flight.
He can strike up a conversation with anyone.
vocab.colloc: strike up a conversation · strike up a friendship

vocab.def: to become more likeable over time.
vocab.use: The thing or person is the subject: “She grew on me.” Never passive.
examples: I disliked the place at first, but it grew on me.
He’s an acquired taste — he grows on you.
vocab.colloc: grow on you · gradually grow on someone

vocab.term: to be on the same wavelength
vocab.def: to understand each other easily.
vocab.use: With “be”, often with “as”: “We’re on the same wavelength as the new director.”
examples: We’ve been on the same wavelength since day one.
They’re just not on the same wavelength.
vocab.colloc: on the same wavelength

vocab.def: to end a long quarrel and make peace.
vocab.use: No object: “They finally buried the hatchet.” Slightly literary but widely understood.
examples: After a decade, the brothers buried the hatchet.
It’s time to bury the hatchet.
vocab.colloc: finally bury the hatchet

grammar.name: Phrasal verbs
grammar.short: Verb + particle, often idiomatic — and sometimes separable.
grammar.rule: A phrasal verb is a verb + one or two particles (up, out, on, up with…) whose meaning is usually idiomatic: you cannot work out ‘put up with’ from ‘put’ + ‘up’ + ‘with’.
form: Separable: turn the TV off / turn off the TV / turn it off.
Inseparable: look after the kids / look after them (never ‘look the kids after’).
Three-part verbs are always inseparable: put up with him, get on with it.
notes: With a PRONOUN object, a separable phrasal verb must split: ‘turn it off’, not ‘turn off it’.
With a long noun phrase, keep the particle close to the verb: ‘She brought up the question of money’ sounds better than ‘brought the question of money up’.
Phrasal verbs are informal; in academic writing the one-word equivalent (tolerate, admire, discover) is often preferred.
examples: We fell out over politics, but we soon made up.
You should look up to people who treat others well.
I just can’t put up with rude behaviour.
grammar.watch: Don’t memorise bare lists. Learn each phrasal verb inside a short sentence that shows who does what to whom.
grammar.deep: Phrasal verbs are best understood as a system of particles rather than a list of items. The particle usually contributes a consistent metaphor: “up” often adds completion or increase (drink up, speak up), “off” separation or cancellation (call off, put off), “out” distribution, exhaustion or discovery (hand out, burn out, find out), “through” endurance (see it through). Once you read the particle, unfamiliar combinations become guessable. The grammar reduces to two facts: whether the verb separates, which the pronoun test settles instantly (“put it off” ✔ / “deal with it” ✔ but never “deal it with”), and whether it takes an object at all. At C1 the discriminating skill is register. Most phrasal verbs have a single-word Latinate equivalent — put off / postpone, look into / investigate, bring about / cause — and choosing the phrasal verb in formal writing, or the Latinate one in casual speech, is what makes a text sound mismatched.

call off, put off, lay off

grammar.name: Gerund & infinitive constructions
grammar.short: Which verbs take -ing, which take to + verb, and which change meaning.
grammar.rule: Some verbs are followed by a gerund (enjoy, avoid, mind, suggest), others by an infinitive (decide, hope, offer, refuse). A small group takes both, with a change of meaning.
form: Verb + -ing: enjoy meeting, avoid arguing, don’t mind waiting.
Verb + to: decide to leave, hope to see, offer to help.
Preposition + -ing (always): interested in meeting, good at listening, instead of calling.
notes: stop doing = end the activity / stop to do = pause in order to do it.
remember to do = don’t forget (future) / remember doing = have a memory (past).
try to do = make an effort / try doing = experiment with it as a solution.
examples: I really enjoy hanging out with my cousins.
She decided to apologise first.
Remember to text me (don’t forget) vs I remember texting you (a memory).
grammar.watch: After a preposition, English always uses -ing: ‘before leaving’, never ‘before to leave’.
grammar.deep: At C1 the gerund/infinitive contrast stops being a list and becomes a semantic tool. The infinitive projects forward — intention, purpose, potential, futurity — which is why it follows verbs of aiming (hope, intend, aim, arrange) and appears after adjectives of evaluation (hard to explain, quick to react). The gerund names an experienced or habitual action, which is why it follows verbs of experiencing (enjoy, resent, tolerate) and every preposition. The productive pairs are where meaning splits: “remember to lock” (a task ahead) versus “remember locking” (a memory behind); “go on to describe” (a new stage) versus “go on describing” (continuation); “I regret to inform” (present bad news) versus “I regret informing” (past action). Perfect and passive forms extend the system further — “to have been chosen”, “having been chosen” — and are essential for compressing time relations in formal writing.

chart.title: Meaning-changing pairs
rows: a task ahead: Remember to call.
a task not done: I forgot to call.
a memory (usually negative): I’ll never forget calling.
pause in order to: We stopped to eat.
make an effort: Try to be early.
move to a new stage: went on to explain
formal bad news: I regret to say

speaking.text: In pairs: two old friends who fell out years ago meet again at a wedding in Cartagena. Rebuild the friendship, disagreeing politely about whose fault it was.
Half the class argues that online friends can be just as close as offline friends; the other half disagrees. Use ‘I see your point, but…’ and ‘I beg to differ’.
Describe your best friend: how did you meet, how did you hit it off, and when do you not see eye to eye?

tips: Disagree politely with softeners: ‘I see what you mean, but…’, ‘I’m not so sure about that’, ‘With respect, I’d say…’.
Learn phrasal verbs in short example sentences, not as bare lists – the context makes the meaning stick.
Common slip: with a pronoun, separable phrasal verbs MUST split – say ‘turn it off’, never ‘turn off it’.

quiz.q: My sister and I ___ over money last year, but we’re fine now.
quiz.explain: ‘Fall out (with someone)’ means to argue and stop being friendly.

units.title: CLOTHES & APPEARANCE

overview.intro: Appearance is a socially delicate topic, so this unit trains you to comment on how people look without sounding rude, and to emphasise what matters to you. Cleft sentences are the key tool: they let you spotlight one idea inside a longer sentence.
goals: Talk about clothes, style and impressions with precise, non-judgemental vocabulary.
Control verb patterns with object + infinitive / object + -ing.
Emphasise a key point using ‘What… is / was…’ structures.
overview.outcome: By the end you can give style advice and defend a position on first impressions, using at least two cleft sentences for emphasis.

vocab.def: to wear smarter clothes / to wear more casual clothes.
vocab.use: ‘Dress up’ can also mean wear a costume, so context matters. ‘Dress down’ is often about a workplace rule (‘dress-down Friday’).
examples: Do we need to dress up for the dinner, or is it casual?
The office lets us dress down on Fridays.
vocab.colloc: dress up for an occasion · dressed up to the nines · a dress-down day

vocab.def: stylish in a subtle, quiet way that doesn’t show off.
vocab.use: A compliment. Its opposites ‘flashy’ and ‘over the top’ are usually criticism.
examples: Her look was understated — one good coat and no jewellery.
He prefers understated elegance to designer logos.
vocab.colloc: understated elegance · an understated look · quietly understated

vocab.def: to wear successfully something that could be hard to wear.
vocab.use: Implies difficulty: only risky clothes need to be ‘pulled off’. It also means ‘succeed at something difficult’ in general.
examples: Not everyone can pull off a bright yellow suit.
She pulled the whole vintage look off perfectly.
vocab.colloc: pull off a look · pull it off · hard to pull off

vocab.def: used clothes passed down from an older person to a younger one.
vocab.use: Usually about siblings or cousins. Neutral to slightly humorous, not insulting.
examples: As the youngest of four, I lived in hand-me-downs.
These jeans are hand-me-downs from my brother.
vocab.colloc: wear hand-me-downs · hand-me-down clothes

vocab.def: someone who starts new fashions that others copy.
vocab.use: Positive. The adjective is ‘trendsetting’; the follower is a ‘follower of fashion’.
examples: Local designers here are real trendsetters.
She was a trendsetter long before the brands noticed.
vocab.colloc: a real trendsetter · a trendsetting designer

vocab.term: to judge a book by its cover
vocab.def: to form an opinion of someone based only on appearance.
vocab.use: Nearly always used as a warning: ‘don’t judge a book by its cover’.
examples: Don’t judge a book by its cover — he’s the best coder here.
We all judge books by their covers, whether we admit it or not.
vocab.colloc: don’t judge a book by its cover

vocab.term: to be dressed to the nines
vocab.def: to be wearing very smart or elaborate clothes.
vocab.use: With “be” or “get”: “everyone was dressed to the nines”.
examples: They arrived dressed to the nines.
There’s no need to be dressed to the nines.
vocab.colloc: dressed to the nines

vocab.def: not affected by changes in fashion.
vocab.use: For designs, garments and style: “a timeless cut”. Contrast with “dated”.
examples: A navy coat is a timeless investment.
Her style is completely timeless.
vocab.colloc: timeless elegance · a timeless classic

vocab.def: to appear suitable for a role or occasion.
vocab.use: No object: “He may be new, but he looks the part.”
examples: In that suit he certainly looks the part.
You don’t have to be an expert; you just have to look the part.
vocab.colloc: look the part · dress the part

vocab.def: stylishness that avoids drawing attention.
vocab.use: A set collocation in fashion writing; uncountable.
examples: The collection is all understated elegance.
She favours understated elegance over logos.
vocab.colloc: understated elegance · quiet luxury

grammar.name: Review of verb patterns
grammar.short: make / let / want / see + object + verb.
grammar.rule: Many verbs are followed by an object plus a verb form. Which form depends on the verb: to-infinitive, bare infinitive, or -ing.
form: Object + to-infinitive: want / expect / tell / advise someone TO do.
Object + bare infinitive: make / let / have someone DO.
Object + -ing or bare infinitive: see / hear / watch someone DO (whole action) or DOING (in progress).
notes: ‘Make’ loses ‘to’ in the active but keeps it in the passive: ‘They made him wait’ → ‘He was made to wait’.
‘Let’ has no passive; use ‘be allowed to’ instead.
Choose -ing to stress that the action was in progress: ‘I saw her trying on the coat’.
examples: I want you to try this jacket on.
The dress code makes everyone wear a suit.
I saw her wearing that exact coat yesterday.
grammar.watch: Never say ‘make someone to do’ in the active voice.
grammar.deep: A verb pattern is a piece of lexical information, and at C1 the task is to control the whole inventory rather than a few families: verb + object + infinitive (persuade her to stay), verb + object + bare infinitive (let him go, make her laugh), verb + object + -ing (catch him cheating), verb + that-clause (insist that he leave), verb + wh-clause (explain what happened), verb + preposition + -ing (accuse her of lying). Errors at this level are rarely random; they come from over-generalising one pattern. “Suggest” and “recommend” resist object + infinitive: “I suggest that you apply” or “I suggest applying”, never “I suggest you to apply”. Verbs of perception change meaning with the form — “I saw him cross” (complete) versus “I saw him crossing” (in progress) — and “help” accepts both bare and marked infinitives with no change at all.

chart.title: Core verb patterns
rows: accuse of, object to, insist on

grammar.name: Cleft sentences with what
grammar.short: Front the key idea: ‘What I love is…’.
grammar.rule: A cleft sentence splits one idea into two clauses so you can spotlight the important part. Put ‘What + clause’ first, then a form of ‘be’, then the highlighted information.
form: What I love about her style IS the confidence.
What really caught my eye WAS the red coat.
What we need IS a look that says ‘professional’.
notes: The verb ‘be’ agrees with what follows it: ‘What I need is a suit’ / ‘What I need are new shoes’.
You can also cleft with ‘It was… that…’ (‘It was the coat that caught my eye’) or ‘All I want is…’.
To highlight an action, use ‘What she did was (to) change…’.
examples: What I love about her style is the confidence.
What really caught my eye was the bright red coat.
What we need is a look that says ‘professional’.
grammar.watch: Use ‘What’, not ‘Which’ or ‘That’, to open this structure.
grammar.deep: A cleft sentence splits one clause into two in order to move the spotlight. “What surprised me was the price” takes an ordinary sentence (the price surprised me) and promotes “the price” to the end, where English puts new or contrastive information. The pattern is “what + clause + be + focus”, and it is one of the most useful tools in argument because it lets you signal what you are challenging: “What we need is not more data but a decision.” Variants extend the range: “All I want is…”, “The thing that bothers me is…”, “It was Ana who called” (an it-cleft, focusing a person), “The reason why they left was…”. Two mechanics: the verb agrees with the “what” clause and is therefore singular, and clefts are for emphasis, so more than one or two in a paragraph makes prose sound theatrical.

chart.title: Cleft structures
rows: What bothers me is the tone.
The tone is what bothers me.
All I asked for was an answer.
It was Ana who noticed it.
It was in May that we signed.
The reason we left is that nobody replied.

speaking.text: In pairs: a personal shopper in a Medellín boutique advises a nervous client on what to wear to an international job interview.
This house believes first impressions matter too much. Argue for or against, using cleft sentences to emphasise your points.
Tell a partner about a time an outfit changed how people treated you. What did you pull off – or fail to pull off?

tips: Use cleft sentences to add emphasis in a presentation: ‘What matters most is…’.
‘Understated’ usually sounds like a compliment; ‘overdressed’ and ‘flashy’ are negative.
Common slip: it’s ‘judge a book BY its cover’, not ‘for its cover’.

quiz.q: ___ really caught my eye was the bright red coat.
quiz.explain: Cleft sentences for emphasis begin with ‘What + clause + be’.

units.title: SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
units.theme: Scientific advances and attitudes toward technology

overview.intro: Talking about science means talking in generalisations — and that is exactly where articles go wrong. This unit fixes a/an, the and zero article, then adds -ing clauses so your writing sounds concise and academic instead of a chain of short sentences.
goals: Discuss innovations, benefits and drawbacks with precise vocabulary.
Use a / an / the / no article correctly with general and specific nouns.
Combine ideas economically with -ing clauses.
overview.outcome: By the end you can present a new technology, weigh its drawbacks, and write a short paragraph using two -ing clauses.

vocab.def: an important discovery or development.
vocab.use: Reserved for genuinely big steps forward — usually in science, medicine or negotiation.
examples: The vaccine was a major breakthrough.
After months of talks, there was finally a breakthrough.
vocab.colloc: a major / scientific / medical breakthrough · make a breakthrough

vocab.def: the most advanced and modern.
vocab.use: Goes before the noun; as a noun phrase say ‘at the cutting edge of’ (no hyphen).
examples: The lab uses cutting-edge imaging equipment.
They are at the cutting edge of battery research.
vocab.colloc: cutting-edge technology / research · at the cutting edge of

vocab.def: to introduce a new product or service gradually.
vocab.use: Suggests stages or regions, not a single launch day. The noun is ‘a rollout’.
examples: They’ll roll the app out city by city.
The rollout starts in Bogotá next month.
vocab.colloc: roll out a service · a nationwide rollout · a phased rollout

vocab.def: something that completely changes a situation.
vocab.use: Common in business and tech talk; slightly overused, so use it for real shifts.
examples: Cheap solar panels were a game-changer for the region.
Remote work has been a game-changer for parents.
vocab.colloc: a real game-changer · prove to be a game-changer

vocab.def: no longer used because something better now exists.
vocab.use: Stronger and more formal than ‘old’: an obsolete device is not just old, it has been replaced.
examples: Fax machines are almost obsolete.
New standards made the old software obsolete overnight.
vocab.colloc: become / render something obsolete · technically obsolete

vocab.def: a disadvantage or problem.
vocab.use: Slightly softer and more analytical than ‘problem’ — ideal for balanced essays.
examples: The main drawback is the price.
Every solution has its drawbacks.
vocab.colloc: the main / only / obvious drawback · have a drawback

vocab.term: to be at the cutting edge
vocab.def: to be at the most advanced stage of development.
vocab.use: “At the cutting edge of + field”. Adjective form: cutting-edge.
examples: The lab is at the cutting edge of gene editing.
They use cutting-edge imaging.
vocab.colloc: at the cutting edge of · cutting-edge research

vocab.def: to grow a system or product to a much larger size.
vocab.use: Both transitive and intransitive in tech usage: “scale the platform”, “it doesn’t scale”.
examples: The model works but it doesn’t scale.
They scaled the service to twenty countries.
vocab.colloc: scale up · hard to scale · scale rapidly

vocab.def: effects nobody planned for.
vocab.use: Almost always plural; the standard phrase in analytical writing about technology.
examples: Every automation has unintended consequences.
The law had serious unintended consequences.
vocab.colloc: unintended consequences of

vocab.def: to make something out of date and useless.
vocab.use: Formal: “render + object + adjective”. Often passive: “was rendered obsolete overnight”.
examples: The update rendered our hardware obsolete.
Fax machines were rendered obsolete years ago.
vocab.colloc: render obsolete · rendered useless

grammar.name: Indefinite & definite articles
grammar.short: a / an, the, and no article at all.
grammar.rule: Use ‘a/an’ to introduce a non-specific singular countable noun, ‘the’ when the noun is specific, already mentioned, or unique, and no article for general plurals and uncountables.
form: First mention, one of many: A breakthrough was announced.
Specific or unique: THE breakthrough we discussed / THE internet / THE sun.
General truth, plural or uncountable: Technology changes fast. Robots are cheaper now.
notes: ‘The’ also appears with superlatives, ordinals and ‘only’: the best result, the first trial, the only option.
Institutions used generally take no article: go to university / be in hospital (UK).
‘a’ vs ‘an’ follows the SOUND: a university, an hour, an MRI scan.
examples: A breakthrough was announced this morning.
The internet has transformed how we learn.
Technology changes faster than laws can keep up.
grammar.watch: Don’t add ‘the’ to a general uncountable: ‘Water is essential’, not ‘The water is essential’.
grammar.deep: Articles encode how you expect your reader to process a noun. “A/an” introduces something new or classifies it; “the” signals that identification is already possible, whether from earlier mention, shared knowledge, a following modifier, or uniqueness; the zero article generalises. That is why a paragraph typically moves from “a study” to “the study”, and why “the lion is a predator” and “lions are predators” are both generic but differ in register. At C1 the residual difficulties are systemic rather than random: abstract nouns take zero for the general concept but “the” when specified (“education matters” / “the education she received”); institutional nouns drop the article when the function is meant (“in hospital”, “at university”) and keep it for the building; and fixed geography rules apply (plural countries and ranges take “the”, single mountains and lakes do not). Reading your own writing for first versus subsequent mention catches most errors.

chart.title: Article decisions
rows: the sun, the CEO, the third floor
the Netherlands, the Andes, but Lake Titicaca

grammar.name: -ing clauses
grammar.short: Compress two sentences into one.
grammar.rule: An -ing clause replaces a full clause of reason, time or accompanying action, as long as both clauses share the same subject.
form: Reason: Feeling curious, she opened the app. (= Because she felt curious…)
Time: Opening the report, he noticed the error. (= When he opened…)
Extra information inside a sentence: The report, showing a clear trend, surprised everyone.
notes: For negatives, put ‘not’ first: Not knowing the password, he gave up.
For an earlier action, use ‘having + past participle’: Having tested the device, they published the results.
If the subjects differ the sentence dangles: ‘Feeling curious, the app was opened’ is wrong.
examples: Feeling curious, the students opened the app.
The report, showing a clear trend, surprised everyone.
Not knowing the password, he gave up.
grammar.watch: Keep the same subject in both halves — that is the number-one -ing clause error.
grammar.deep: An -ing clause compresses a whole subordinate clause into a participle phrase, and formal English uses it constantly to signal cause, result, accompaniment or sequence without a conjunction. “Having reviewed the data, the team revised its forecast” marks completion; “Realising the error, she called immediately” marks cause; “Sales fell sharply, forcing a rethink” marks result and is placed after the main clause; “She left, taking the file with her” marks accompaniment. Two rules govern legality. The implied subject of the participle is the subject of the main clause, so mismatches produce dangling modifiers — “Walking into the room, the lights were off” makes the lights walk. And the negative goes before the participle (“not knowing the answer”). For passive relations, use the past participle or “being + participle”: “Written in 1890, the novel still reads well.”

chart.title: -ing clauses and what they signal
rows: Sitting at the back, I heard nothing.
Being new, she asked a lot of questions.
Costs doubled, wiping out the margin.
Built in 1890, the bridge still stands.
Walking in, the lights were off. ✘

speaking.text: Two engineers pitch a new app to investors at a Bogotá startup expo. The investors keep asking about the drawbacks.
Artificial intelligence will do more good than harm. Take a side and defend it with examples.
Tell a partner about one piece of technology you couldn’t live without – and one you think is already obsolete.

tips: Say ‘the internet’, ‘the environment’ – these take ‘the’. But general ‘technology’ / ‘science’ take no article.
-ing clauses make writing sound more advanced – use them to combine two short sentences.
Common slip: don’t add ‘the’ to a general uncountable – ‘Water is essential’, not ‘The water is essential’ (in general).

quiz.q: ___ internet has completely changed the way we study.
quiz.explain: ‘The internet’ is a unique thing, so it takes the definite article ‘the’.

units.title: SUPERSTITIONS & BELIEFS

overview.intro: Beliefs are usually somebody else’s claims, so this unit is built on reporting: what people say, what is said in general, and how much distance you keep from the claim. Impersonal passive reporting is the C1 skill that makes you sound objective.
goals: Describe superstitions, hoaxes and levels of belief accurately.
Report speech with correct tense, pronoun and time-word shifts.
Use impersonal passive reporting (‘It is said that…’) to stay neutral.
overview.outcome: By the end you can interview someone, then report their claims to a third person without taking a side.

vocab.def: a belief that certain actions bring good or bad luck.
vocab.use: The adjective ‘superstitious’ describes the person: ‘He’s very superstitious’.
examples: There’s a superstition here about yellow underwear at New Year.
She dismisses it all as pure superstition.
vocab.colloc: an old / local superstition · be superstitious about something

vocab.def: a sign that something good or bad will happen.
vocab.use: Usually with ‘good’ or ‘bad’. The adjective ‘ominous’ always means threatening.
examples: Rain on your wedding day is a good omen in some cultures.
They took the power cut as a bad omen.
vocab.colloc: a good / bad omen · an omen of things to come

vocab.def: a trick that makes people believe something untrue.
vocab.use: Bigger and more deliberate than a joke, and often public: a fake photo, a false alarm.
examples: The photo turned out to be an elaborate hoax.
Someone made a hoax call to the fire service.
vocab.colloc: an elaborate hoax · a hoax call · turn out to be a hoax

vocab.def: too ready to believe things, and so easily fooled.
vocab.use: Mildly critical. About the person; ‘far-fetched’ is about the story.
examples: The scam targets gullible investors.
I’m too gullible — I believe everything I read.
vocab.colloc: be gullible enough to · prey on gullible people

vocab.def: very unlikely to be true.
vocab.use: Use for explanations and stories, not people.
examples: His excuse sounded pretty far-fetched.
It seems far-fetched, but the evidence supports it.
vocab.colloc: a far-fetched story / theory / excuse · sound far-fetched

vocab.def: to prove that a belief or story is false.
vocab.use: Formal and journalistic; the object is a myth, claim or theory — not a person.
examples: Scientists debunked the claim within a week.
The channel debunks viral health myths.
vocab.colloc: debunk a myth / theory / claim · widely debunked

vocab.term: to take something at face value
vocab.def: to accept a claim as it appears, without questioning it.
vocab.use: Common in critical discussion: “I wouldn’t take that at face value.”
examples: Don’t take the testimony at face value.
At face value, the claim seems reasonable.
vocab.colloc: take it at face value · at face value

vocab.def: to make a claim seem more believable.
vocab.use: Formal: “The photograph lends credence to her account.”
examples: Nothing lends credence to that theory.
The data lends credence to the hypothesis.
vocab.colloc: lend credence to · give credence to

vocab.def: based on personal stories rather than research.
vocab.use: Almost always with “evidence”: “the evidence is purely anecdotal”.
examples: The support is anecdotal at best.
Anecdotal evidence isn’t proof.
vocab.colloc: anecdotal evidence · purely anecdotal

vocab.def: to say that something was said, written or caused by someone.
vocab.use: “Attribute X to Y”, often passive: “The quotation is wrongly attributed to Twain.”
examples: The rise is attributed to lower rates.
The remark was attributed to an unnamed official.
vocab.colloc: widely attributed to · wrongly attributed

grammar.name: Reporting clauses
grammar.short: Tense, pronoun and time shifts after said / told.
grammar.rule: When you report what someone said earlier, the verb usually moves one step back in time, and pronouns, places and time words change to fit your point of view.
form: is / are → was / were; do → did; will → would; can → could.
have done / did → had done.
today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; here → there; this → that.
notes: ‘Say’ takes no personal object (He said that…); ‘tell’ requires one (He told ME that…).
No shift is needed if the statement is still true: ‘She says the ritual works’.
Reporting verbs carry attitude: admit, claim, insist, deny, warn — choose one that signals how reliable the claim is.
examples: He admitted (that) he had broken the mirror.
She told me she would never walk under a ladder.
They claimed the house was haunted.
grammar.watch: Reported questions lose the question word order: ‘She asked where I was’, not ‘where was I’.
grammar.deep: A reporting clause does two jobs at once: it transmits content and it evaluates it. Choosing “state”, “claim”, “allege”, “concede”, “insist” or “admit” tells your reader how much credibility to extend, and at C1 that choice is assessed as closely as the tense shifts. Beyond the verb, the position of the reporting clause matters — placing it mid-sentence (“The findings, the authors argue, are preliminary”) subordinates the attribution and keeps the content in focus. Backshift remains the mechanical layer, and it is optional when the reported information is still true or the report is immediate; keeping the present tense (“the report says that inflation is easing”) actively signals current relevance. Watch the patterns: “claim”, “argue” and “insist” take that-clauses; “accuse” takes “of + -ing”; “deny” takes a gerund; and “report” and “say” differ in whether they permit an object.

grammar.name: Reporting clauses in the passive
grammar.short: ‘It is said that…’ / ‘He is believed to…’.
grammar.rule: Impersonal passive reporting removes the source of a claim, which makes the statement sound neutral and academic.
form: It + be + said / believed / thought / claimed + that + clause.
Subject + be + said / believed + to + infinitive: He is believed to be innocent.
For an earlier action: He is thought TO HAVE FAKED the whole thing.
notes: Use it when the source is unknown, obvious or unimportant.
‘Reportedly’ and ‘allegedly’ do a similar job in one word.
In speech this can sound distant; in essays and news writing it is standard.
examples: It is said that black cats bring bad luck.
The ritual is believed to protect the home.
He is thought to have faked the whole thing.
grammar.watch: ‘It says that…’ is not the passive — you need ‘It IS SAID that…’.
grammar.deep: Passive reporting clauses remove the source and foreground the claim: “It is thought that the practice began in the 1600s”, or the raised alternative, “The practice is thought to have begun in the 1600s”. Academic and journalistic prose relies on them when the source is a diffuse consensus, unknown, or deliberately unnamed — which is exactly why a critical reader treats them with suspicion. Two structures cover the ground. The impersonal “it” version (it is said / believed / estimated / reported that…) keeps the clause intact. The subject-raising version promotes the subject of the reported clause and follows with an infinitive, using the perfect infinitive for earlier time: “He is believed to have left the country.” Note that a few verbs, notably “say”, appear almost exclusively in the raised passive rather than the active, which is why “he is said to be wealthy” has no natural active equivalent.

chart.title: Passive reporting structures
rows: It is believed that talks have stalled.
She is thought to live abroad.
He is said to have refused the offer.
It was reported that the deal collapsed.
They are believed to be negotiating.
It is estimated that / are estimated to

speaking.text: A journalist interviews a self-proclaimed psychic. Afterwards, report to the class what the psychic claimed, using reported speech.
Superstitions are harmless fun and nobody is really hurt by them. Agree or disagree.
Share a superstition from your family or region with a partner. Where does it come from, and do you believe it?

tips: Use ‘It is said / believed / thought that…’ to sound impersonal and academic.
In reported speech, shift the tense back: is → was, will → would, have done → had done.
Common slip: after ‘say’ you don’t need an object (He said that…); after ‘tell’ you do (He told me that…).

quiz.q: In impersonal reports we say: It ___ that walking under a ladder is unlucky.
quiz.explain: The passive reporting structure is ‘It is said that…’.

units.title: MOVIES & TELEVISION
units.theme: Movie and TV trends, genres and reviews

overview.intro: Reviewing is an opinion genre, so this unit gives you tools for attitude and intensity: sentence adverbs that comment on the whole statement, and so/such structures that push an adjective to its consequence.
goals: Review films and series with genre-specific vocabulary.
Comment on a whole statement using sentence adverbs.
Express cause and result with so…that / such…that.
overview.outcome: By the end you can give a two-minute spoiler-free review with clear attitude markers and at least two result structures.

vocab.def: an unexpected change in the story.
vocab.use: Often ‘a twist’ on its own. The verb form: ‘the plot twists’.
examples: The plot twist in the last ten minutes changes everything.
I saw the twist coming from the first scene.
vocab.colloc: a clever / predictable plot twist · see a twist coming

vocab.def: information that reveals what happens and ruins the surprise.
vocab.use: Warn people with ‘spoiler alert’ or promise ‘no spoilers’.
examples: No spoilers, please — I’m only on episode two.
Spoiler alert: someone doesn’t make it.
vocab.colloc: a spoiler alert · avoid spoilers · spoiler-free review

vocab.def: to watch many episodes one after another.
vocab.use: Very current, always about series. The noun is ‘a binge’.
examples: We binge-watched the whole season in a weekend.
I try not to binge-watch on weeknights.
vocab.colloc: binge-watch a series · a weekend binge

vocab.def: a very successful, expensive film.
vocab.use: About commercial size, not quality — a blockbuster can still be bad.
examples: Another superhero blockbuster opens this Friday.
The studio needs a blockbuster to survive.
vocab.colloc: a summer blockbuster · a box-office blockbuster

vocab.def: praised more than it deserves.
vocab.use: Strong opinion word; soften it with ‘a bit’ or ‘slightly’. Opposite: underrated.
examples: Honestly, that series is wildly overrated.
It’s a bit overrated, but still enjoyable.
vocab.colloc: wildly / hugely overrated · vastly underrated

vocab.def: so exciting that it holds your full attention.
vocab.use: For plots, books and performances; not for people.
examples: The first season is absolutely gripping.
A gripping thriller with a superb cast.
vocab.colloc: a gripping thriller / drama · utterly gripping

vocab.def: to reveal something that should stay secret.
vocab.use: Separable: “don’t give it away”. Also “give away the ending”.
examples: I won’t give away the ending.
One review gave the whole twist away.
vocab.colloc: give away the ending · give the game away

vocab.def: inconsistent in quality.
vocab.use: With “be”: “The second season is hit and miss.”
examples: His films are hit and miss.
The service here is a bit hit and miss.
vocab.colloc: hit and miss · rather hit and miss

vocab.def: praised by professional critics.
vocab.use: Before a noun: “a critically acclaimed drama”. Contrast with “commercially successful”.
examples: The series was critically acclaimed but barely watched.
Her critically acclaimed debut won three awards.
vocab.colloc: critically acclaimed film · widely acclaimed

vocab.def: to accept an unrealistic story while watching it.
vocab.use: Usually “willing suspension of disbelief” or “you have to suspend disbelief”.
examples: You have to suspend disbelief for the first ten minutes.
It asks too much suspension of disbelief.
vocab.colloc: suspend disbelief · suspension of disbelief

grammar.name: Sentence adverbs
grammar.short: Comment on the whole sentence, not the verb.
grammar.rule: A sentence adverb tells the listener your attitude to the whole statement — how certain, how honest, how surprising it is.
form: Front position + comma (most common): Frankly, the ending disappointed me.
Mid position between commas: The ending, frankly, disappointed me.
End position after a comma: The ending disappointed me, frankly.
notes: Honesty: frankly, honestly, to be fair. Certainty: apparently, presumably, undoubtedly. Reaction: surprisingly, unfortunately, luckily.
Contrast with adverbs of manner: ‘She spoke frankly’ describes HOW she spoke; ‘Frankly, she spoke…’ comments on the statement.
One per sentence — stacking them sounds cluttered.
examples: Frankly, the ending was a huge disappointment.
Apparently, they are already filming a sequel.
Surprisingly, the low-budget film won.
grammar.watch: Don’t forget the comma; without it the meaning shifts to manner.
grammar.deep: Sentence adverbs comment on the whole proposition rather than on the verb, and they are one of the clearest markers of an advanced writer because they encode stance economically. Different subsets do different work: evaluation (fortunately, regrettably, remarkably), certainty (undoubtedly, presumably, arguably), viewpoint (technically, financially, statistically), and discourse framing (admittedly, incidentally, ultimately). Position carries meaning: initial position frames everything that follows, mid position is unobtrusive, and final position reads as an afterthought. The one to handle carefully is “hopefully”, still contested in the sentence-adverb sense in conservative registers, and “arguably”, which is a hedge and not a synonym of “clearly”. Punctuation is consistent: a comma in initial position, commas both sides in mid position, and no comma when the adverb modifies the verb rather than the sentence — compare “Frankly, she refused” with “She refused frankly”.

chart.title: Sentence adverbs by function
rows: Ironically, the sequel outsold the original.

grammar.name: such…that / so…that
grammar.short: Degree plus result.
grammar.rule: Both structures link a high degree to its consequence. ‘So’ goes with an adjective or adverb alone; ‘such’ goes with a noun phrase.
form: so + adjective/adverb + that: It was so confusing that nobody understood.
such + (a/an) + adjective + noun + that: It was such a long film that I fell asleep.
so much / so many + noun + that: There were so many twists that I lost track.
notes: ‘That’ can be dropped in speech: ‘It was so long I fell asleep’.
‘so much’ for uncountables, ‘so many’ for countables.
For formal emphasis you can invert: ‘So confusing was the plot that…’.
examples: It was such a long film that I fell asleep.
The plot was so confusing that nobody understood it.
She acted so convincingly that she won an award.
grammar.watch: ‘so boring film’ is wrong — with a noun you need ‘such a boring film’.
grammar.deep: “So … that” and “such … that” express a degree that produces a result, and the only difference is what follows: “so” takes an adjective or adverb (“so long that we left”), “such” takes a noun phrase (“such a long film that we left”). Once that is fixed, three refinements repay attention. With quantity words, “so” attaches to much, many, few and little (“so many twists that I lost track”). The “that” is frequently omitted in speech but retained in careful writing. And an inverted, emphatic variant exists in formal register: “So convincing was the performance that the audience gasped” — a structure worth recognising because it appears often in reviews and academic prose. Note also that “such” can appear without a result clause as a pure intensifier (“it was such a disappointment”), where the result is implied.

chart.title: so … that / such … that
rows: It was so slow that I left.
It was such a slow film that I left.
They were such long scenes that…
so much / many / few / little + that
There were so many twists that I lost track.
So gripping was the ending that nobody moved.

speaking.text: Two film critics on a talk show review a new blockbuster – one loved it, the other thinks it’s overrated.
Streaming platforms have ruined the cinema experience. Argue for or against.
Recommend a film to your partner without spoilers, using ‘so’ and ‘such’: ‘It was so gripping that…’.

tips: Put a comma after a sentence adverb at the start: ‘Honestly, I didn’t like it.’
Remember: ‘such + (adjective) noun’, but ‘so + adjective’ alone.
Common slip: avoid ‘so much + countable’ – say ‘so many twists’, not ‘so much twists’.

quiz.q: The film was ___ boring that half the audience left.
quiz.explain: Before an adjective on its own we use ‘so…that’; ‘such’ needs a noun.

units.title: MUSICIANS & MUSIC
units.theme: Musical tastes, artists and defining success

overview.intro: Music is about change over time — tastes, careers, technology. The grammar matches: double comparatives express two things changing together, and will/would describe habits then and now.
goals: Talk about taste, talent and success in the music industry.
Link two changing variables with ‘the more…, the more…’.
Describe present and past habits with will and would.
overview.outcome: By the end you can trace how your taste has changed and argue a case about the music industry with comparative structures.

vocab.def: easy to remember and pleasant to hum.
vocab.use: Positive but light — about the hook, not artistic depth.
examples: The chorus is incredibly catchy.
It’s a catchy tune, but the lyrics are weak.
vocab.colloc: a catchy tune / chorus / hook · annoyingly catchy

vocab.def: unable to hear the difference between musical notes.
vocab.use: Also used figuratively for someone who misreads a social situation: ‘a tone-deaf statement’.
examples: I’m completely tone-deaf, so I only listen.
The apology was tone-deaf and made things worse.
vocab.colloc: completely tone-deaf · a tone-deaf response

vocab.def: to spread very quickly online.
vocab.use: The subject is the content, not the person: ‘her video went viral’.
examples: The clip went viral overnight.
One remix went viral and changed his career.
vocab.colloc: go viral overnight · a viral hit · go viral on TikTok

vocab.def: an artist famous for only a single successful song.
vocab.use: Slightly dismissive; can also refer to the song itself.
examples: Critics wrote them off as a one-hit wonder.
She proved she was no one-hit wonder.
vocab.colloc: be dismissed as a one-hit wonder

vocab.def: the words of a song.
vocab.use: Almost always plural, with a plural verb. The writer is a ‘lyricist’.
examples: The lyrics are surprisingly political.
I misheard the lyrics for years.
vocab.colloc: the lyrics are… · write lyrics · clever / cheesy lyrics

vocab.def: to sell all the tickets for a show.
vocab.use: Two meanings: sell every ticket (positive) or abandon your principles for money (very negative).
examples: The concert sold out in ten minutes.
Fans accused the band of selling out.
vocab.colloc: sell out a stadium · a sold-out show · sell out to a label

vocab.def: to resonate emotionally with people.
vocab.use: “Strike a chord with + audience”: “The lyrics struck a chord with a whole generation.”
examples: The song struck a chord with young listeners.
Her speech struck a chord.
vocab.colloc: strike a chord with · touch a nerve

vocab.def: to be forgotten after a period of fame.
vocab.use: Intransitive: “The band faded into obscurity.” Opposite: “rise to prominence”.
examples: Most one-hit wonders fade into obscurity.
He faded into obscurity within a decade.
vocab.colloc: fade into obscurity · sink into obscurity

vocab.def: copying an existing style without originality.
vocab.use: Critical: “The album is derivative.” Noun use is different (finance, linguistics).
examples: Critics called the record derivative.
It’s competent but derivative.
vocab.colloc: largely derivative · derivative of

vocab.term: to stand the test of time
vocab.def: to remain valued for many years.
vocab.use: Usually with “have”: “Few albums have stood the test of time like this one.”
examples: The record has stood the test of time.
Not every classic stands the test of time.
vocab.colloc: stand the test of time

grammar.name: Double comparatives
grammar.short: ‘The more…, the better…’.
grammar.rule: Use two comparatives, each introduced by ‘the’, to show that as one thing changes the other changes with it.
form: The + comparative + clause, the + comparative + clause: The more you practise, the better you get.
Short form with no verb: The louder the crowd, the happier the band.
With nouns: The more tickets they sell, the bigger the venue.
notes: ‘The’ is obligatory in both halves.
In short forms the verb ‘be’ is often left out.
‘More and more’ / ‘better and better’ shows continuous change in one variable: ‘Concerts are getting more and more expensive’.
examples: The more you practise, the better you get.
The louder the crowd, the happier the band.
The harder the song, the more rewarding it is.
grammar.watch: ‘More you practise, better you get’ is wrong — both halves need ‘the’.
grammar.deep: Double comparatives express proportional change — as one variable moves, so does another — and English does it with a matched pair: “the + comparative, the + comparative”. Both halves are clauses, so a full version reads “The louder the music got, the fewer people stayed”, and a reduced version drops the verbs entirely: “the sooner, the better”. Two related structures belong to the same family: the repeated comparative for gradual change (“the queues got longer and longer”, “more and more expensive”) and “as … so …” in formal register (“as the audience grew, so did the ticket prices”). Two mechanics: the comparative must be attached to whatever word it modifies, including quantity words (“the more tickets we sold”), and the second clause is the consequence, which means reversing the halves reverses your claim.

chart.title: Proportional and gradual change
rows: The longer the tour, the higher the costs.
The more people came, the better it felt.
The sound got louder and louder.
more and more / less and less
Tickets became more and more expensive.
As demand rose, so did prices.

grammar.name: will & would for habits
grammar.short: Typical behaviour now and in the past.
grammar.rule: ‘Will’ describes present habits and general truths; ‘would’ describes repeated past actions, often with a nostalgic tone.
form: Present habit: He’ll listen to the same album for weeks.
General truth: Water will boil at 100°C at sea level.
Past habit: When I was young, I would hum along to everything.
notes: Stressed ‘will’ shows irritation: ‘He WILL play it at full volume’.
‘Would’ works with actions, not states — for states use ‘used to’: ‘I used to love that band’.
‘Used to’ covers both actions and states, so it is the safer choice when unsure.
examples: He’ll listen to the same album on repeat for weeks.
Water will boil at 100°C at sea level.
When I was young, I would hum along to everything.
grammar.watch: Never ‘I would love it’ for a past state — say ‘I used to love it’.
grammar.deep: “Will” and “would” are not only future and conditional markers; both describe characteristic behaviour. Present “will” states a general truth or a typical habit, often with a note of resignation or criticism when stressed: “Musicians will always complain about venues.” Past “would” narrates repeated past behaviour in an established time frame: “After every show he would sit alone for an hour.” The constraint that separates “would” from “used to” is that “would” cannot describe a past state — “he would be shy” is not a habit but a conditional. Two further notes for C1: stressed “will” in the present can convey exasperation about a person’s repeated behaviour (“she will insist on driving”), and “would” in this habitual sense requires a scene to be set first, which is why it appears in the second or third sentence of a narrative rather than the first.

chart.title: Habitual will and would
rows: She used to be a session player.

speaking.text: A band manager negotiates a slot at a music festival with the organiser – discuss the fee, the time and the stage.
Streaming platforms pay musicians fairly. Agree or disagree, with reasons.
Tell a partner how your music taste has changed: ‘I would only listen to… but now I’ll…’.

tips: The double comparative always needs ‘the’ twice: ‘the more, the better’ – not ‘more, better’.
‘Would’ for past habits works with actions, not states – say ‘I used to love it’, not ‘I would love it’.
Common slip: ‘lyrics’ is normally plural – ‘the lyrics are…’, not ‘the lyrics is…’.

quiz.q: ___ you practise, the better you become.
quiz.explain: Double comparatives use ‘the + comparative’ in both halves: ‘The more…, the better…’.

units.title: CHANGING TIMES

overview.intro: This unit compares generations, which means defining people and things precisely — the job of relative clauses — and comparing how things are done, the job of as if / the way. Together they let you describe change without vagueness.
goals: Discuss generational change, upbringing and milestones.
Decide when a relative pronoun can be omitted.
Compare real and imagined manner with as if / as though / the way.
overview.outcome: By the end you can narrate how life in your city has changed across two generations, using relative clauses accurately.

vocab.def: to start a stable, calmer life, often with a family.
vocab.use: Also means ‘become calm’ (‘settle down, class!’). Context decides.
examples: They travelled for years before settling down.
He has no plans to settle down yet.
vocab.colloc: settle down and start a family · ready to settle down

vocab.def: the way a person is raised as a child.
vocab.use: Uncountable-ish: use ‘a strict upbringing’, never ‘upbringings’ as a plural list.
examples: She had a strict Catholic upbringing.
Their upbringing taught them to save.
vocab.colloc: a strict / religious / privileged upbringing

vocab.def: the difference in attitudes between older and younger people.
vocab.use: Usually with ‘the’ and ‘between’.
examples: The generation gap shows most clearly online.
There’s a real generation gap between us on work.
vocab.colloc: bridge / close the generation gap

vocab.def: a sentimental longing for the past.
vocab.use: Uncountable. The adjective ‘nostalgic’ goes with ‘about’ or ‘for’.
examples: The song fills me with nostalgia.
I feel nostalgic about those summers.
vocab.colloc: a wave of nostalgia · nostalgia for the nineties

vocab.def: to remember and reflect on the past.
vocab.use: Three parts, so inseparable: ‘look back on it’, never ‘look it back on’.
examples: Looking back on it, I made the right choice.
She looks back on those years fondly.
vocab.colloc: look back on something fondly / with regret

vocab.def: an important event or turning point in life.
vocab.use: For life events and project stages alike: graduation, a first job, a product launch.
examples: Graduating was a huge milestone for my family.
We hit every milestone this quarter.
vocab.colloc: reach / hit a milestone · a major life milestone

vocab.def: an event marking an important stage of life.
vocab.use: Countable: “a rite of passage”. Common in writing about generations.
examples: Getting your first job is a rite of passage.
The trip became a rite of passage for the family.
vocab.colloc: a traditional rite of passage

vocab.def: to recall or resemble an earlier time.
vocab.use: Inseparable, followed by a noun: “a design that harks back to the 1970s”.
examples: The film harks back to a gentler era.
He’s always harking back to his student days.
vocab.colloc: hark back to the past

vocab.def: having a strong influence on how someone developed.
vocab.use: Usually before a noun: “formative years”, “a formative experience”.
examples: Those were my formative years.
It was a formative influence on her writing.
vocab.colloc: formative years · a formative experience

vocab.def: knowing now what you did not know then.
vocab.use: Interchangeable with “in hindsight”; pairs with past modals and unreal conditionals.
examples: With hindsight, we changed too fast.
With hindsight, I’d have waited.
vocab.colloc: with hindsight · with the benefit of hindsight

grammar.name: Optional & required relative pronouns
grammar.short: When you can drop who / that / which.
grammar.rule: In a defining relative clause you may omit the pronoun when it is the OBJECT of that clause, but you must keep it when it is the SUBJECT.
form: Object → optional: the book (that) I read; everything (that) she said.
Subject → required: the man WHO called; the app THAT crashed.
Non-defining clauses (with commas) always keep the pronoun: My aunt, who lives in Cali, called.
notes: Test it: remove the pronoun. If a verb is left stranded with no subject, the pronoun was the subject and must stay.
‘Whose’ is never omitted: the family whose house we bought.
In careful writing, move the preposition to the front: ‘the house in which we grew up’; in speech it stays at the end.
examples: The house (that) we grew up in has been sold.
The neighbour who moved in is very friendly.
Everything (that) she said turned out to be true.
grammar.watch: Never use ‘that’ in a non-defining clause after a comma — use who / which.
grammar.deep: Whether a relative pronoun can be dropped depends entirely on the job it does inside its own clause. As subject it is obligatory, because deleting it leaves the clause without a subject: “the woman who called” cannot become “the woman called”. As object it is optional, because the clause already has a subject: “the film (that) we watched”. Two further conditions apply. In non-defining clauses the pronoun is never omitted, since the commas already signal a suspension of the main clause. And when a preposition is involved, omission is possible only if the preposition stays at the end: “the colleague I spoke to” ✔, “the colleague to whom I spoke” ✔ (formal), but never “the colleague to I spoke”. At C1, deliberate omission is a fluency marker: overusing “that” makes prose plod, while omitting it in the object slot tightens the rhythm.

chart.title: When can the relative pronoun be dropped?
rows: My boss, who joined in May, …
the writer whose work we studied

grammar.name: as if / as though / the way / like
grammar.short: Comparing manner, real and imagined.
grammar.rule: Use ‘as if / as though’ for an appearance or an imagined situation, and ‘as / the way’ to compare how something is actually done.
form: as if / as though + clause: It looks as though the plan has changed.
Unreal comparison → past form: He spends money as if he WERE a millionaire.
as / the way + clause: Do it the way your teacher explained.
notes: A present tense after ‘as if’ suggests the appearance may be real; a past form marks it as clearly unreal.
‘Like’ + noun is standard (‘like a millionaire’); ‘like’ + clause is informal.
‘As’ + clause is formal: ‘As we discussed, prices have risen’.
examples: He spends money as if he were a millionaire.
Do it the way your teacher explained.
It looks as though the plan has changed.
grammar.watch: In exams and writing, prefer ‘as if’ to ‘like’ before a clause.
grammar.deep: “As if” and “as though” introduce a comparison with an imagined or apparent situation, and they are followed by a clause: “He talks as if he owned the place.” The tense choice carries the speaker’s judgement — a past form after a present verb signals that the comparison is contrary to fact, while a present form leaves it open: “It looks as if it’s working” (possibly true) versus “He behaves as if he were in charge” (he isn’t). “Like” does the same job informally and, in careful writing, prefers a noun rather than a clause: “like a professional” rather than “like he was a professional”. “The way” is a neutral alternative for manner (“she writes the way she speaks”), and “as” alone introduces a clause of manner in formal register (“as I explained earlier”), where using “like” would lower the register.

chart.title: as if / as though / the way / like
rows: It looks as if we’re late.
He acts as if he knew everything.
He talks like he owns it.
Do it the way I showed you.
As I mentioned, the deadline moved.

speaking.text: A grandparent and a grandchild discuss how daily life has changed since the grandparent was young.
Life was simpler and better before smartphones. Argue for or against.
Describe a personal milestone and how it changed you, using ‘nostalgia’ and ‘look back on’.

tips: If you can remove the relative pronoun and the sentence still works, it was the object – so it’s optional.
After ‘as if / as though’, a past tense signals something imaginary: ‘as if he were rich’.
Common slip: in careful English, use ‘as if’ rather than ‘like’ before a clause.

quiz.q: She spends money ___ she were a millionaire.
quiz.explain: ‘As if’ (+ past tense) describes an unreal or imagined situation.

units.title: CONSUMER CULTURE

overview.intro: Shopping and complaining are transactional situations where word order and formality matter. This unit covers how to arrange two objects around a verb, and the subjunctive you need for firm, formal requests and recommendations.
goals: Discuss consumer habits, marketing and value with precise vocabulary.
Order direct and indirect objects naturally.
Use the subjunctive after insist, recommend, demand and ‘it is essential that…’.
overview.outcome: By the end you can haggle, complain and make a formal written recommendation using the subjunctive correctly.

vocab.def: something bought suddenly, without any planning.
vocab.use: The adverb phrase is ‘on impulse’: ‘I bought it on impulse’.
examples: The jacket was a total impulse buy.
Shops put sweets by the till to encourage impulse buys.
vocab.colloc: a total impulse buy · buy on impulse · impulse purchase

vocab.def: the tendency to keep buying the same brand.
vocab.use: Marketing vocabulary; the person is ‘loyal to’ a brand.
examples: Brand loyalty is falling among younger shoppers.
He’s fiercely loyal to that brand.
vocab.colloc: build / lose brand loyalty · strong brand loyalty

vocab.def: to argue about a price until you both agree.
vocab.use: Use ‘over’ for the thing and ‘with’ for the person. Normal at markets, rude in supermarkets.
examples: We haggled over the price for ten minutes.
She haggled with the vendor and got it half price.
vocab.colloc: haggle over the price · haggle with a seller

vocab.def: something bought for much less than its usual price.
vocab.use: ‘A bargain’ is the item; ‘a good deal’ is the transaction. Both are positive.
examples: At that price it’s an absolute bargain.
I picked up a real bargain in the sales.
vocab.colloc: an absolute / real bargain · a bargain price · bargain hunting

vocab.def: a culture that encourages buying more and more goods.
vocab.use: Usually critical, common in essays. The adjective is ‘consumerist’.
examples: The film is a critique of modern consumerism.
Black Friday is consumerism at its peak.
vocab.colloc: rampant / mass consumerism · a consumerist society

vocab.def: the specific group a product is aimed at.
vocab.use: Also ‘target market’. The verb: a campaign ‘targets’ a group.
examples: Our target audience is students under 25.
The ad missed its target audience completely.
vocab.colloc: identify / reach a target audience · aimed at a target market

vocab.def: cheap at first but more expensive in the long run.
vocab.use: “Buying the cheapest one is a false economy.” Countable with “a”.
examples: Skipping maintenance is a false economy.
It’s a false economy to hire the cheapest supplier.
vocab.colloc: a false economy

vocab.def: to cause prices or demand to rise.
vocab.use: Separable: “drive prices up”, “drive up demand”. Opposite: “drive down”.
examples: Scarcity drives up prices.
The campaign drove demand up by a third.
vocab.colloc: drive up prices · drive down costs

vocab.def: the money you have left to spend after tax and essentials.
vocab.use: Uncountable: “rising disposable income”. A standard term in market analysis.
examples: Disposable income has stagnated.
Luxury sales track disposable income closely.
vocab.colloc: rising disposable income · limited disposable income

vocab.def: to be convinced by an idea or product.
vocab.use: Usually with “be”, often negative: “I’m not sold on the redesign.”
examples: I’m not entirely sold on the strategy.
She was sold on it after one demo.
vocab.colloc: not sold on it · completely sold on

grammar.name: Placement of direct & indirect objects
grammar.short: give me the receipt / give the receipt to me.
grammar.rule: Verbs like give, send, show and offer take two objects. You can put the person first with no preposition, or the thing first followed by to / for.
form: Verb + indirect + direct: The clerk gave me a refund.
Verb + direct + to/for + indirect: The clerk gave a refund to me.
With two pronouns, prefer the to-form: Send it to her.
notes: Put new or emphasised information last — that usually decides which order sounds natural.
‘Explain, describe, suggest’ never take the person directly: ‘explain the rule TO me’, not ‘explain me the rule’.
‘Buy / make / find’ use ‘for’, not ‘to’: I bought a gift for her.
examples: The clerk gave me a refund.
The clerk gave a refund to me.
Send it to her (rather than ‘send her it’).
grammar.watch: ‘Explain me the problem’ is a very common error — always ‘explain the problem to me’.
grammar.deep: With two objects, English chooses the order according to weight and information status. The double-object pattern puts the recipient first with no preposition (“she gave the client a discount”); the prepositional pattern puts the thing first and the recipient last with to or for (“she gave a discount to the client”). Three factors decide. Pronouns go early because they are light: “give it to her” rather than “give her it”, and never “give to her it”. New or long information goes last, which is why the prepositional pattern suits recipients that need explaining (“she sent the file to the auditor who requested it”). And some verbs are restricted: explain, describe, suggest, mention and announce reject the double-object pattern altogether — “explain me the rule” is a persistent error where only “explain the rule to me” is possible.

chart.title: Object placement
rows: She sent the contract to me.
He gave the file to the new analyst.
I saved a seat for you.
or: I saved you a seat.

grammar.name: Verbs in the subjunctive
grammar.short: insist / recommend / it is essential + base form.
grammar.rule: After verbs and expressions of demand, advice or importance, the verb in the that-clause stays in its base form for every subject — no -s, no tense.
form: insist / suggest / recommend / demand / request + that + subject + BASE VERB.
it is essential / vital / important + that + subject + BASE VERB.
Negative: We insist that he NOT be charged.
notes: The base form does not change with he/she/it: ‘that she arrive’, ‘that he be refunded’.
British English often prefers ‘should’: ‘We recommend that she should try a smaller size’.
‘Suggest’ and ‘recommend’ also take -ing: ‘We recommend trying a smaller size’.
examples: The manager insisted that the customer be refunded.
It is essential that every receipt be kept.
We recommend that she try a smaller size.
grammar.watch: Never ‘suggest to do’ — use ‘suggest that he apply’ or ‘suggest applying’.
grammar.deep: The English subjunctive survives in a narrow but high-register set of structures, and using it accurately is a clear C1 marker. After verbs and nouns of demand, recommendation and necessity — insist, demand, recommend, suggest, propose, request, essential, vital, imperative — the that-clause takes the bare base form regardless of person or tense: “The board insists that he resign”, “It is vital that she be informed.” Note the two visible consequences: no third-person -s, and “be” rather than “is”. British English often prefers “should” in the same slot (“insists that he should resign”), and both are correct. The other survival is the past subjunctive “were”, used in unreal conditions and after “wish” for all persons: “if I were you”, “as though he were joking”. Fixed formulaic remnants — “be that as it may”, “suffice it to say”, “God forbid” — are worth recognising rather than producing.

chart.title: Subjunctive triggers
rows: She proposed that the vote be delayed.
It is vital that everyone attend.
They insisted that he should apologise.
We ask that visitors not enter.

speaking.text: Haggle at a market stall in Cartagena: one student is the vendor, the other is a tourist trying to get a bargain.
Advertising manipulates us into buying things we don’t need. Agree or disagree.
Describe your last impulse buy to a partner. Was it a bargain or a waste of money?

tips: In the subjunctive the verb is always the base form – ‘he be’, ‘she arrive’ – with no -s.
With two pronouns choose the ‘to’-form: ‘give it to me’, not ‘give me it’.
Common slip: after ‘suggest’ use ‘that + subjunctive’ or ‘-ing’ – ‘suggest that he apply’ / ‘suggest applying’, never ‘suggest to apply’.

quiz.q: It is essential that every employee ___ present at the meeting.
quiz.explain: After ‘it is essential that…’ we use the base form (subjunctive): ‘be’.

units.title: NATURE
units.theme: Animals, ethics and the natural world

overview.intro: Environmental discussion needs generalisation: any place, any time, anyone. The ‘-ever’ words do exactly that, and they also build noun clauses that can act as subject or object — a compact, advanced structure.
goals: Talk about wildlife, conservation and ethics accurately.
Distinguish when/where from whenever/wherever.
Build noun clauses with whoever, whatever, whichever.
overview.outcome: By the end you can brief a group on protecting a habitat and argue an ethical case using at least three ‘-ever’ structures.

vocab.def: at serious risk of no longer existing.
vocab.use: For species and languages. Stronger stages: ‘critically endangered’, then ‘extinct’.
examples: The cotton-top tamarin is critically endangered.
Several endangered species live in that reserve.
vocab.colloc: an endangered species · critically endangered · endangered habitat

vocab.def: the natural home of an animal or plant.
vocab.use: Countable. ‘Habitat loss’ is the standard term for destruction.
examples: Mangroves are a vital habitat for young fish.
Habitat loss is the biggest threat here.
vocab.colloc: natural habitat · habitat loss / destruction · restore a habitat

vocab.def: to hunt or catch animals illegally.
vocab.use: The person is a ‘poacher’; the crime is ‘poaching’. Also used for hiring staff from rivals.
examples: Gangs poach turtle eggs from the beach.
Rangers arrested two poachers last night.
vocab.colloc: poach for ivory · illegal poaching · anti-poaching patrol

vocab.def: the protection of nature and wildlife.
vocab.use: Uncountable. ‘Conservation’ protects; ‘preservation’ keeps unchanged.
examples: She works in marine conservation.
Conservation efforts have doubled the population.
vocab.colloc: wildlife / marine conservation · conservation efforts · a conservation area

vocab.def: the variety of living things in an area.
vocab.use: Uncountable — never ‘biodiversities’. Colombia is one of the most biodiverse countries on earth.
examples: The Amazon holds extraordinary biodiversity.
Monoculture farming reduces biodiversity.
vocab.colloc: rich / high biodiversity · biodiversity loss · a biodiversity hotspot

vocab.def: a community of living things and their environment.
vocab.use: Countable; often ‘a fragile ecosystem’. Also used metaphorically in business.
examples: The páramo is a fragile ecosystem.
Removing one predator can unbalance the whole ecosystem.
vocab.colloc: a fragile / delicate ecosystem · disrupt an ecosystem

vocab.def: to gradually take over land or territory.
vocab.use: “Encroach on habitat / land / rights”. Formal, common in environmental writing.
examples: Farming has encroached on the forest.
New building is encroaching on wetlands.
vocab.colloc: encroach on habitat · gradual encroachment

vocab.term: to be on the brink of
vocab.def: very close to a serious change, usually bad.
vocab.use: “On the brink of extinction / collapse”. Followed by a noun or -ing.
examples: The species is on the brink of extinction.
The reef is on the brink of collapse.
vocab.colloc: on the brink of extinction

vocab.def: the ability of a system or person to recover.
vocab.use: Uncountable: “ecological resilience”, “build resilience”. Adjective: resilient.
examples: Diversity increases a system’s resilience.
The forest has shown remarkable resilience.
vocab.colloc: build resilience · ecological resilience

vocab.def: to balance one effect with an opposite one.
vocab.use: Transitive: “offset emissions”. Past form is also “offset”.
examples: Tree planting offsets some emissions.
The gains offset the losses.
vocab.colloc: offset emissions · offset the cost

grammar.name: whenever / wherever vs when / where
grammar.short: Specific time and place, or any at all.
grammar.rule: ‘When’ and ‘where’ point to one particular time or place. Adding ‘-ever’ makes it ‘at any time / in any place’, or shows that the exact one does not matter.
form: Specific: They return to the beach WHERE they were born.
Any / every: They nest WHEREVER the sand is warm enough.
Concession (‘it doesn’t matter’): Wherever you look, there is plastic.
notes: ‘-ever’ clauses never use ‘will’ after them: ‘Call whenever you SPOT the birds’.
‘No matter when / where’ is a common paraphrase.
‘Whenever’ can also mean ‘every time that’: ‘Whenever it rains, the river rises’.
examples: Sea turtles return to the beach where they were born.
They nest wherever the sand is warm enough.
Call me whenever you spot the birds.
grammar.watch: Don’t use a future tense inside the -ever clause.
grammar.deep: “Whenever” and “wherever” differ from “when” and “where” by generalising: they mean “at any time that” and “at any place that”, so they describe a rule rather than an occasion. “When I visit the park, I take my camera” reports a habit tied to a known event; “Whenever I visit a park, I take my camera” claims it is invariably true. This is why “whenever” pairs naturally with statements of policy and pattern, and why it can also express indifference to the specific time: “Come whenever you like.” Two further points: “wherever” takes the same generalising role for place and appears in concessive clauses (“wherever you go, take a map”), and in careful writing these forms take the present simple even for future reference, following the ordinary rule for time clauses — “whenever the results arrive, I’ll forward them”.

chart.title: when/where vs whenever/wherever
rows: When I got home, I called her.
Whenever I get home, I call her.
Wherever we go, we take the dog.
Whenever the data arrives, I’ll check it.

grammar.name: Noun clauses with whoever / whatever
grammar.short: ‘Any person / thing that…’ as subject or object.
grammar.rule: ‘Whoever, whatever, whichever’ introduce a clause that works like a noun — it can be the subject or the object of the main verb.
form: As subject: WHOEVER LITTERS HERE will be fined.
As object: Take WHATEVER YOU NEED.
With a noun: The centre helps WHATEVER ANIMAL arrives.
notes: The verb after a subject ‘whoever’ is singular: ‘Whoever wants to help is welcome’.
‘Whomever’ exists for object position but sounds very formal; ‘whoever’ is normal.
‘Whichever’ implies a limited set of choices; ‘whatever’ is open.
examples: Whoever litters here will be fined.
The rescue centre helps whatever animal arrives.
We’ll support whoever protects the reserve.
grammar.watch: Don’t add a second subject: ‘Whoever litters here, HE will be fined’ is wrong.
grammar.deep: “Whoever”, “whatever”, “whichever” and “however” build noun clauses that name an unspecified person, thing or manner: “Whoever wrote this understood the problem.” The clause fills a noun slot, so it can be the subject, the object or the complement, and it keeps statement word order throughout. Two mechanical points repay attention. Case follows the role inside the clause, not outside: “whoever asks” (subject) but “whomever we appoint” in formal writing (object) — although modern usage widely accepts “whoever” in both. And the same words also form concessive clauses meaning “it doesn’t matter who/what”: “Whatever you decide, I’ll support you.” The difference is functional: a noun clause fills a slot, while a concessive clause is an adverbial you could delete. Reading the sentence without the clause tells you which one you have written.

chart.title: whoever / whatever clauses
rows: Whoever signed it made an error.
Whichever route we take, it’s far.
However hard we try, it fails.

speaking.text: A park ranger briefs a group of international tourists before a hike in Tayrona National Park.
Zoos do more harm than good for wildlife. Argue for or against.
Tell a partner about one endangered animal you would protect and why, using ‘whatever’ and ‘wherever’.

tips: ‘-ever’ words add flexibility: whenever = at any time, wherever = in any place.
‘whoever / whatever’ can be the subject or object of their clause: ‘Whoever calls…’ / ‘Call whoever you like.’
Common slip: Colombia is one of the most biodiverse countries – use ‘biodiversity’ (uncountable), never ‘biodiversities’.

quiz.q: Take ___ you need from the supply box.
quiz.explain: ‘Whatever’ = any thing that; it introduces a noun clause as the object of ‘take’.

units.title: LANGUAGE
units.theme: Effective communication and attitudes toward language

overview.intro: When you write about language, the doer is often unknown or irrelevant — which is what the passive is for. This unit systematises the passive across tenses and then tackles the agreement problems quantifiers create.
goals: Talk about fluency, dialect, register and communication strategies.
Form and choose the passive across tenses, including ‘have something done’.
Make verbs agree correctly after quantifiers like none of, a number of, each of.
overview.outcome: By the end you can write an objective paragraph about language use in your country with accurate passives and agreement.

vocab.def: able to speak a language easily and well.
vocab.use: Fluent = smooth, not necessarily error-free. Use ‘fluent IN Portuguese’.
examples: She’s fluent in three languages.
He speaks fluent but heavily accented English.
vocab.colloc: fluent in a language · become fluent · fluent speaker

vocab.def: a form of a language spoken in a particular region.
vocab.use: A dialect has its own grammar and vocabulary; an ‘accent’ is only pronunciation.
examples: Costa Rican and Colombian Spanish differ in dialect.
The play is written in a regional dialect.
vocab.colloc: a regional / local dialect · speak in dialect

vocab.def: very informal words used by a particular group.
vocab.use: Uncountable: ‘a piece of slang’, not ‘a slang’. Avoid in formal writing.
examples: Teenage slang changes every year.
Some slang doesn’t travel between cities.
vocab.colloc: street / teenage slang · use slang · slang expression

vocab.def: the first language you learned as a child.
vocab.use: Also ‘native language’ or ‘L1’. Some people have two.
examples: My mother tongue is Spanish, but I dream in English sometimes.
Teaching is best in a child’s mother tongue at first.
vocab.colloc: mother-tongue speaker · in your mother tongue

vocab.def: to learn it informally, without lessons.
vocab.use: Suggests ease and no study. Separable: ‘pick it up’.
examples: He picked up Italian while working in Rome.
Kids pick languages up incredibly fast.
vocab.colloc: pick up a language / an accent / a few phrases

vocab.def: to make people understand what you mean.
vocab.use: About successful communication despite limited words — exactly what a C1 speaker needs.
examples: I don’t know all the words, but I get my point across.
Use examples to get your point across faster.
vocab.colloc: get your point across clearly · struggle to get your point across

vocab.def: to manage to pronounce something difficult.
vocab.use: Usually negative or with “can’t”: “I can’t get my tongue around that name.”
examples: I still can’t get my tongue around it.
It took a week to get my tongue around the word.
vocab.colloc: get your tongue around a word

vocab.def: to speak a language easily and accurately.
vocab.use: “Fluent in Spanish”, not “fluent Spanish” as a predicate. Noun: fluency.
examples: She’s fluent in three languages.
He’s fluent but not accurate.
vocab.colloc: fluent in · near-native fluency

vocab.def: a word borrowed from another language.
vocab.use: Two words or hyphenated; countable: “English is full of loan words.”
examples: “Patio” is a Spanish loan word in English.
Loan words often change meaning.
vocab.colloc: a loan word from · borrow a word

vocab.def: to lose meaning when moved between languages.
vocab.use: Usually passive: “The humour is lost in translation.”
examples: The wordplay is lost in translation.
Something always gets lost in translation.
vocab.colloc: lost in translation

grammar.name: Overview of passives
grammar.short: be + past participle, across all tenses.
