grammar.rule: Use the passive when the action or its result matters more than who performed it, or when the agent is unknown, obvious or deliberately hidden.
form: Present: English IS SPOKEN here. Past: The report WAS WRITTEN last week.
Perfect / future / modal: has been published, will be translated, must be signed.
Causative: I HAD my essay CHECKED by a tutor.
notes: Add ‘by + agent’ only when the doer adds information.
Only transitive verbs have a passive — ‘happen’ and ‘arrive’ cannot be passive.
Overusing the passive makes writing heavy; mix it with active sentences.
examples: Over 60 languages are spoken in Colombia.
The report was written last week.
I had my essay checked by a tutor (have something done).
grammar.watch: Don’t drop ‘be’: ‘The report written last week’ is not a full passive sentence.
grammar.deep: The passive is a discourse tool, and a C1 overview means controlling it across every tense and structure, not just the simple ones. The pattern is always a form of “be” plus a past participle, with the tense living entirely in “be”: is written, was written, is being written, has been written, will be written, is going to be written, must be written, to be written, having been written. The passive is chosen for three reasons: the agent is unknown or irrelevant; the object is the topic and belongs in subject position for cohesion; or the writer wants to background responsibility. Two constraints: only transitive verbs can be passivised, so happen, arrive, occur and die have no passive; and verbs with two objects allow two passives, of which the recipient version is far more natural (“I was sent the report” rather than “the report was sent me”).

chart.title: Passive across tenses and forms
rows: It had been agreed in advance.
You will be notified. / It must be signed.

grammar.name: Subject-verb agreement with quantifiers
grammar.short: Which noun does the verb follow?
grammar.rule: After quantifiers with ‘of’, the verb normally agrees with the noun that follows ‘of’ — but a few phrases have fixed behaviour.
form: Some / most / all / half of + singular → singular verb; + plural → plural verb.
Each / every one / neither / either of + plural noun → SINGULAR verb.
A number of + plural → plural verb; THE number of + plural → singular verb.
notes: ‘None of’ takes either: ‘none of it is’, ‘none of them are’ — both accepted.
Don’t let a long phrase between subject and verb confuse you: ‘The list of new words IS long’.
‘There is / are’ agrees with the first noun after it.
examples: None of the homework was difficult.
A number of students were absent.
Each of the answers is correct.
grammar.watch: ‘Each of the students ARE’ is wrong — ‘each’ is always singular.
grammar.deep: Agreement with quantified subjects is decided by the noun that follows the quantifier, not by the quantifier itself, and this is where careful writers slip. “Most of the data is” treats data as a mass; “most of the files are” treats files as countable. Fractions and percentages behave the same way: “half of the budget has gone” but “half of the seats have gone”. Some quantifiers are fixed regardless: “each”, “every”, “either”, “neither” and “none of” (in careful writing) take a singular verb; “both”, “several” and “a number of” take a plural. Two frequent traps: “the number of X is” but “a number of X are”, and a long prepositional phrase between subject and verb (“the list of participants who registered late”) which tempts a plural verb where the head noun, “list”, is singular.

chart.title: Subject–verb agreement with quantifiers
rows: Most of the evidence is circumstantial.
Most of the students are bilingual.
Each of the entries has a code.
None of the data is complete.
A number of speakers are missing.
The number of speakers is falling.
The list of names is on the desk.

speaking.text: The organiser of a language-exchange meetup welcomes international students and explains the ground rules.
English is becoming too dominant as a global language. Agree or disagree.
Tell a partner about a time you couldn’t find a word – how did you get your point across?

tips: Use the passive to sound objective, or when the doer is obvious or unknown: ‘The results were published.’
‘A number of’ takes a plural verb; ‘the number of’ takes a singular verb.
Common slip: ‘none of’ can take a singular OR plural verb – both ‘none of it is’ and ‘none of them are’ are accepted.

quiz.q: A number of students ___ absent from class today.
quiz.explain: ‘A number of’ + plural noun takes a plural verb: ‘were’.

units.title: EXCEPTIONAL PEOPLE
units.theme: Role models, values and high achievers

overview.intro: Describing remarkable people economically is the goal here. Compound adjectives pack a whole description into one hyphenated word, and their superlatives let you rank people precisely instead of repeating ‘very’.
goals: Describe character, achievement and resilience with strong vocabulary.
Build compound adjectives and hyphenate them correctly.
Form superlatives of compound adjectives.
overview.outcome: By the end you can introduce a role model in a short speech using at least four compound adjectives, one of them superlative.

vocab.def: a person others admire and try to copy.
vocab.use: Two words, no hyphen. Often ‘a positive role model FOR young people’.
examples: Teachers are role models whether they like it or not.
She’s a positive role model for young athletes.
vocab.colloc: a positive / poor role model · a role model for someone

vocab.def: to admire and respect someone.
vocab.use: Three parts, inseparable: ‘look up to her’. Opposite: ‘look down on’ (despise).
examples: I’ve always looked up to my grandmother.
Younger players look up to him.
vocab.colloc: look up to a parent / mentor · look down on someone

vocab.def: firmly decided to succeed and not give up.
vocab.use: Followed by ‘to + verb’. The noun is ‘determination’.
examples: She was determined to finish the degree.
His determination impressed everyone.
vocab.colloc: determined to succeed · fiercely determined · sheer determination

vocab.def: able to recover quickly from difficulties.
vocab.use: For people, communities and systems. Noun: ‘resilience’.
examples: Small businesses here are remarkably resilient.
Resilience matters more than talent in the long run.
vocab.colloc: remarkably resilient · build resilience · a resilient community

vocab.def: to succeed in dealing with a problem.
vocab.use: Irregular: overcome – overcame – overcome.
examples: She overcame serious injuries to compete again.
They overcame every obstacle in their way.
vocab.colloc: overcome an obstacle / a fear / adversity

vocab.def: new and very different in an important way.
vocab.use: One word, no hyphen. For work, research and art — not people.
examples: Her groundbreaking research changed the field.
A groundbreaking album for its time.
vocab.colloc: groundbreaking research / work / discovery

vocab.def: to be the first to do something others then follow.
vocab.use: “Blaze a trail for + group”. Noun: trailblazer.
examples: She blazed a trail for women in engineering.
They blazed a trail that others followed.
vocab.colloc: blaze a trail for · a trailblazer

vocab.def: despite very low chances of success.
vocab.use: Usually at the start or end: “Against all odds, she qualified.”
examples: Against all odds, the project succeeded.
She recovered against all odds.
vocab.colloc: against all odds · defy the odds

vocab.def: having learned without formal instruction.
vocab.use: Hyphenated, before or after the noun: “a self-taught pianist”, “he is entirely self-taught”.
examples: She’s a self-taught programmer.
Most of the team is self-taught.
vocab.colloc: entirely self-taught · a self-taught artist

vocab.def: to leave lasting influence behind you.
vocab.use: “Leave a legacy of + noun”: “a legacy of reform”. Countable.
examples: He left a legacy of open-access research.
Her legacy is still visible in the curriculum.
vocab.colloc: leave a lasting legacy · a legacy of

grammar.name: Compound adjectives
grammar.short: Two words, one hyphen, one meaning.
grammar.rule: A compound adjective joins two or more words into a single describing word placed before a noun, normally with a hyphen.
form: adjective/adverb + participle: quick-thinking leader, well-known scientist, hard-working student.
number + singular noun: a five-year plan, a ten-page report.
noun + adjective: a world-famous athlete, a sugar-free drink.
notes: Hyphenate before the noun; after the verb the hyphen usually disappears: ‘the singer is well known’.
Adverbs ending in -ly are NOT hyphenated: ‘a highly respected expert’.
The number stays singular: ‘a five-year plan’, never ‘a five-years plan’.
examples: She is a quick-thinking leader.
They signed a three-year contract.
He is a world-famous athlete.
grammar.watch: Missing hyphens change meaning: ‘a well known author’ vs ‘a well-known author’.
grammar.deep: Compound adjectives fuse two or more words into a single pre-noun modifier, and English hyphenates them precisely because the hyphen shows which words belong together: “a well-known writer” versus “a well known writer”, where the second reads as an adverb modifying a separate adjective. Several productive patterns account for most of them: adverb + past participle (well-designed, widely-read), noun + past participle (award-winning is noun + present participle; hand-made is noun + past participle), adjective + noun + -ed (short-tempered, open-minded), and number + noun in the singular (a five-year plan, a ten-minute break — never “five-years”). Two rules of usage matter. Hyphenate before the noun but usually not after it: “a well-known author” but “the author is well known”. And compounds formed with -ly adverbs take no hyphen at all: “a highly regarded study”.

rows: a five-year plan, a two-hour delay

grammar.name: Superlative compound adjectives
grammar.short: best-known, hardest-working, most widely respected.
grammar.rule: To make a compound adjective superlative, put the superlative on the FIRST element, or use ‘most’ when the first element cannot take -est.
form: First element takes -est / best / worst: the hardest-working student, the best-known artist.
With ‘most’: the most highly regarded expert, the most widely respected award.
Comparative works the same way: a better-known writer, a harder-working team.
notes: Say ‘best-known’, not ‘most well-known’, in careful English.
Keep the hyphen in the superlative form: ‘the best-known’.
Add ‘in / of’ to limit the comparison: ‘the hardest-working person ON the team’.
examples: She is the best-known writer of her generation.
He is the hardest-working person on the team.
It is the most widely respected award in the field.
grammar.watch: Never double the superlative: ‘the most hardest-working’ is wrong.
grammar.deep: Compound adjectives take superlatives in two ways, and the choice depends on where the gradable element sits. When the compound begins with an adverb or an adjective that can itself be compared, the comparison usually falls on that first element: best-known, worst-paid, longest-serving, highest-earning. When no element is gradable in that way, English puts “most” in front of the whole compound: the most award-winning studio, the most open-minded colleague. A third possibility is to attach “most” to the whole phrase for emphasis even where an inflected form exists, though this can read as clumsy. Note the fixed spellings: better-known and best-known, not “more known”, and the hyphen is retained in the superlative. As with all compounds, the hyphen disappears after the noun: “she is the best known of the three” keeps it, because the compound still modifies an implied noun.

speaking.text: At an award ceremony, introduce a national hero (for example a Colombian scientist, athlete or artist) to an international audience.
Natural talent matters more than hard work. Argue for or against.
Describe someone you look up to, using at least three compound adjectives (hard-working, open-minded, quick-thinking…).

tips: Hyphenate before a noun: ‘a well-known singer’; but after the verb, drop it: ‘the singer is well known’.
Say ‘best-known’, not ‘most well-known’, for the superlative.
Common slip: keep the first number singular – ‘a five-year plan’, not ‘a five-years plan’.

quiz.q: Gabriel García Márquez is the ___ writer Colombia has produced.
quiz.explain: The standard superlative compound adjective is ‘best-known’.

units.theme: Entrepreneurship, negotiation and the ideal job

overview.intro: The final unit is about professional register. Conditional inversion (‘Should you need…’) is the single fastest way to sound formal in emails and interviews, and adverb clauses of condition let you set precise terms in a negotiation.
goals: Discuss startups, negotiation and career priorities with business vocabulary.
Replace ‘if’ with inversion in formal conditionals.
Set conditions with provided that, as long as, unless and in case.
overview.outcome: By the end you can run a negotiation and write a formal follow-up email using inversion and at least two conditional linkers.

grammar.name: Subject-verb inversion in conditionals
grammar.short: Were I you… / Had we known… / Should you need…
grammar.rule: In formal English you can delete ‘if’ and invert the subject with were, had or should. The meaning is identical; the register is higher.
form: If I were in charge → WERE I in charge, I would raise salaries.
If we had invested → HAD WE invested earlier, we would have profited.
If you should need help → SHOULD YOU need help, please email us.
notes: Only were, had and should invert — you cannot say ‘Wanted I a raise…’.
Negatives are not contracted: ‘Had we not invested…’, never ‘Hadn’t we invested…’.
‘Should you…’ is standard in business emails for polite offers of help.
examples: Were I in charge, I would raise salaries.
Had we invested earlier, we would have profited.
Should you have any questions, please email us.
grammar.watch: Keep it for writing and formal speech; in casual conversation it sounds stiff.
grammar.deep: Formal English can drop “if” and invert the subject and auxiliary instead, producing a structure that appears constantly in contracts, reports and academic prose. Three patterns cover it: “Should you require assistance, please call” (first conditional with should), “Were we to accept the offer, we would need board approval” (second conditional with were + to), and “Had we known the risk, we would have withdrawn” (third conditional). Note what inverts: the auxiliary only, and only should, were and had — you cannot invert “did” or “would”, so “Did I have time…” is not a conditional inversion. In the negative, the full form is required: “Had we not known”, never “Hadn’t we known”, since the contracted version would read as a question. These forms are more formal than their if-equivalents, and mixing one into casual speech sounds affected rather than polished.

chart.title: Inverted conditionals
rows: Were we to accept the offer,
If it had not been for you,
Had it not been for you,

grammar.name: Adverb clauses of condition
grammar.short: provided that, as long as, unless, in case.
grammar.rule: These linkers state the condition under which something is true, and each carries a slightly different nuance.
form: provided (that) / as long as = only if this is true: You can leave early provided the work is done.
unless = if not: Unless sales improve, we’ll cut costs.
in case = as a precaution: Take a card in case you need to pay.
notes: ‘In case’ ≠ ‘if’: ‘Take a card in case’ (a precaution) vs ‘Take a card if you need it’ (only then).
No future tense in the condition clause: ‘as long as you HIT the target’.
Don’t use a second negative after ‘unless’.
examples: You’ll get the bonus as long as you hit the target.
Unless sales improve, we’ll cut costs.
Take a card in case you need to pay.
grammar.watch: ‘Unless you don’t hurry’ is a double negative — say ‘Unless you hurry’.
grammar.deep: Beyond “if”, English has a graded inventory of conditional conjunctions, and each one narrows the condition differently. “Provided that” and “on condition that” impose a requirement. “As long as” does the same, more informally. “Unless” means except if and carries the negative itself. “Only if” makes the condition exclusive and, when it opens the sentence, triggers inversion in the main clause: “Only if the board approves will we proceed.” “Even if” concedes that the condition will not change the outcome. “In case” marks a precaution taken before the event, and “whether or not” cancels the condition altogether. Two mechanics govern them all: no “will” inside the conditional clause, and a comma when the clause comes first. Choosing precisely among them is what makes conditional writing sound legally and logically tight rather than merely hypothetical.

chart.title: Adverb clauses of condition
rows: Provided that funding arrives, we start in May.
You can stay as long as you contribute.
Unless they agree, the deal collapses.
Only if they agree will we proceed.
Even if they agree, it’s too late.
Keep a copy in case the system fails.
We’ll proceed whether or not they agree.

tips: Inversion (‘Were I you…’) sounds formal – great for writing and interviews.
‘provided that’ and ‘as long as’ both mean ‘only if this condition is true’.
Common slip: after ‘unless’ don’t add a second negative – ‘Unless you hurry…’ (not ‘Unless you don’t hurry…’).
